header.title: De Inventione Capitis Joannis Baptistae: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Dionysius Exiguus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0108f.stoa005.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0108f.stoa005.opp-l: Scanning errors silently corrected throughout (e.g. 'Gau lentio' Gaudentio, 'diviuo nota' divino nutu, 'ablatura Emesenæ' ablatum Emesenam, 'cupit expelli' cœpit expelli). In the last line 'cum quen' is read as 'eum quem'. 'Non enim potuit impetrare ne id quod moliebatur efficeretur' is awkward; taken as: his request was refused, so that his scheme (apparently to remove or hide the relic) did not succeed. 'Alterius sectæ' (of another sect) presumably means a heretical, anti-Nicene group; the text does not name it. 'Vas eremi pretiosissimum' (the most precious vessel of the desert) is taken to mean the Baptist's head.

The year 'septuagesimo sexagesimo tertio' is garbled; the variant 'septingentesimo' gives 763, presumably of the Seleucid era (= AD 452/3); translated as 763. 'Universalis apostolus' and 'ter beatissimus' are as printed, applied to John. 'Peritius' is the Macedonian month name. 'Thrice most blessed... there appeared' leaves the appearance's object implicit in the Latin. 'Sub clave archimandritae' and the clause 'et sic ingressus est' (Palladius finally got in) read awkwardly; the sense of the third visit is uncertain. Variants noted by the edition (e.g. 'ad pectus' for 'ad pedes') were not followed. Scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. saticti, En.esenae, Diensis, niOlio, PIItefecit, Scbastc).

Line 9: the edition prints variant readings in brackets ('al., oravimus' for 'adoravimus'; 'al., Daramium' for Claramnium; 'Salius' for Saltus; 'al., Marius' for Maris; 'al., Malachus' for Malchus); these are left out of the English. 'mundissimorum palum' read as 'panum' (loaves); 'eras' read as 'cras' (tomorrow); 'adde vis' supplies 'multitude'. The bracket after 'per te' gives an alternative wording ('tomorrow at sunrise'). 'Caperelo', 'collectarius' (perhaps a collector or money-changer) and 'Linopola Lechtarius' (taken as linen-seller and litter-bearer) are uncertain. A footnote mark 'a' before 'Facta est' is omitted. The year 763 is presumably in a local (Seleucid?) era; 'Valentinian the Younger' with Marcian is historically odd (Valentinian III would fit). Line ab5 heads a separate sermon translated by Combefis, not by Dionysius.

The edition passes from section 20 to 22; section 21 is missing in the text supplied, so there may be a gap here. In 16, 'pigris' is read as 'pignus'; in 19, 'agnina' as 'agmina' (companies), and 'alria' as 'atria'. 'Mediae hebdomadae jejuniorum' presumably means the middle week of Lent. 'Concha' is taken as a niche or apse-like recess. In 15, 'prius area educat, quam ille nuntiet vitae exitum' is obscure ('ille' may refer to the gift itself signalling her death); rendered loosely. Marcellus's first-person narrative begins in 18 without a clear closing of the quotation; I have kept it open through 22.

Line 23: the narrative is still in Marcellus's first person, so opening quotation marks continue as in the preceding lines; the first-person account ends within line 24, and from line 25 the voice is that of the later author recounting the third finding. Line 25: 'acus nomine' is evidently a damaged name; rendered '[Mal]chus' after the earlier Malchus in this work, but the reading is uncertain. Line 26: 'nemqe', 'ticri', 'aHio' and similar are scanning errors for 'nempe', 'fieri', 'alio'. Line 28: 'Theophoro illi cognomini' alludes to the patriarch Ignatius sharing his name with Ignatius Theophorus of Antioch. The reference to 'three changes of things, which they call earthquakes' is obscure. Ref .29 is absent from the sequence.

Line 37: 'sinque Joannis tollit caput' is evidently corrupt; read as 'si non Joannis tollit caput' ('even if it does not take off John's head'), which the following 'at' requires. Line 41: 'arctor' read as 'artor' ('I am constrained'). Line 34: 'stellarum varientem' read as 'varietatem'. The comparison clause 'pari cum eis nomine ac gloria certantis' (line 39) is obscure; rendered tentatively.

nodes.text: DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS: ON THE FINDING OF THE HEAD OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST
PROLOGUE.
To the lord Abbot Gaudentius, whom I revere, Dionysius [sends greeting].

The care and zeal of the dearest brothers whom you govern by the grace of Christ have compelled [me] to render through my own pen, in Latin speech, the account of the finding of the head of blessed John the Baptist which was written in the Greek tongue. They said it was fitting that on the feast of him, than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women, this account handed down about him should be made known to the faithful peoples. So with a ready mind I set out what was asked, though in a short time, above all because I learned that your holiness also wished this same thing to be done. Nor do I see that this has come about without a divine nod. The same holy John, forerunner of the Lord, herald of truth, summit of all the prophets and founder of monks, showed himself first to monks, who carried off his most holy head from the house of Herod, the once impious king; then, when it had been taken to Emesa and lay unknown for long ages, he again made himself known to monks. In the same way he has now deigned to make this history about himself known to the Romans through the service of monks, however lowly. He takes delight, I believe, in the service of the venerable way of life, so that through those who follow the solitary life he might make his glory in Christ known. And we say this not to claim insolently for ourselves the awareness of some distinguished mind, but because the devout profession of itself displays a holy zeal, even if our slothful manner of life does not match it. And who among the faithful could be unaware what manner of life that most blessed man then led? For beyond that extraordinary bounty of the divine gift by which he was conceived according to the promise, while still enclosed in his mother's womb, from the womb which [God] had made fruitful when barren, he recognised the Author of the universe in the womb of the holy Virgin. Beyond that singular glory too by which he became the Baptist of Christ and the friend of the heavenly bridegroom, he often stayed alone in deserted and hidden places, persevering day and night in fasting and prayer, clothed in camels' hair, and fed on locusts and wild honey. All these are shown to be signs of the utmost continence and frugality, by which, renouncing the whole world with its pomps and pleasures, he deigned to see nothing other than Christ; to whom also, as he came to his baptism, he bore witness, saying, Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world. And although by such distinguished and magnificent deeds he set examples of virtue before all, yet the chief men with the elders, the scribes and the Pharisees reproached his merits with insane audacity; to which our Lord testifies in the Gospel, and said: John the Baptist came neither eating nor drinking, and you say: He has a demon. Just so now many Christians, without doubt very like the Pharisees, if they happen to see servants of God practising abstinence, do not shrink from bursting out into the same abuse and curses, and from pursuing with their insults the thing they ought to attain by imitation: so that a commendable life, exposed to malicious rumours, may be able to hold to a praiseworthy perseverance, by which it may kindle the fervour of the old emulation. We endure this hatred because of likeness of conduct, so that what our Lord says in the Gospel is proved true in us also: If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of this world, therefore the world hates you. Saint John, whose festival is celebrated today by the Church throughout the whole world, met these hatreds of the world, and even in the times of Julian, a tyrant rather than a prince, he endured them in the rest of his body, which, as the most holy Gospels relate, was then given burial by his disciples. For the savage cruelty of the pagans, in keeping with the character of the most impious apostate Julian, broke open the most blessed man's tomb, madly dragged out his bones, burned them with fire, reduced them to dust, and scattered them everywhere in insane fury. But the grace of Christ, which directs the hearts of its servants, had in those days brought to that very place from Jerusalem, for the sake of prayer, monks who, seeing so wicked a crime committed by the impious, while the pagans themselves stood astonished, carried off those venerable relics and at once set out from there, bearing the venerable treasure with them. Behold, again the service of monks is divinely arranged, so that just as the head of this saint was found through monks, so also through monks the remaining relics of his body should be preserved. These were at once sent to Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria; and afterwards Theophilus, bishop of the same city, while destroying all the shrines of the idols, deposited them amid the great veneration of the people in the basilica which he built with pious devotion in the name of the same most blessed John the Baptist. But it is now time that we relate to you the aforesaid history, and in return for this labour of ours effectively obtain the support of your prayers.
ON THE FINDING OF THE HEAD OF JOHN THE BAPTIST.
On the first finding of the precious head of the illustrious and glorious prophet, the forerunner John the Baptist. Dionysius Exiguus translator.

Two monks set out from the East, desiring to see the precious cross of Christ and the glorious tomb of him who for our salvation was made man and endured death, through which he bestowed on us life and immortality, and also the venerable places of his resurrection and ascension into heaven; and they came to Jerusalem. To one of them the forerunner of the Lord's coming and baptist of the eternal King, Saint John, appeared standing by and said: "Go to what was once the house of King Herod, and take away with you my head, which you will find buried in the ground." When morning had risen, the monk told his brother the vision he had seen; the other, suspecting a delusion of fancy, persuaded the one to whom the mystery had been revealed to think as he did, that it was nothing. When they had let the matter drop, on the next day the herald of truth stood by each of them separately and, appearing to them alike, spoke thus: "Drive all doubt of unbelief out of your hearts, and let your thinking not limp with regard to the truth of the vision." And when each had told the other of the agreement, strengthened by the twofold vision and fearing punishment for disobedience, they fulfilled without delay what had been commanded them. With divine grace going before them, they placed the head of the Baptist, which had been cut off for justice and piety, in a sack of haircloth. And I reckon the prophet was pleased with such a covering, whose body had once been clothed in the desert with camels' hair. So the monks were returning, carrying the head which Herodias, receiving it on a dish as the reward for her dancing daughter, had won like the longed-for spoil of a hunt. Indeed, thinking that the rebukes of the prophet's tongue had now ceased, she would by no means allow that venerable head to be buried with the rest of the body, conceiving fear of their joining, and doubtless reasoning that the saint's whole body would rise with all ease, but that this could not happen if she herself kept the head. And therefore she did not give it to burial just anywhere, but buried it within the precincts of her own house. For the love of an unlawful union, betrayed by its own devices, fashioned for itself images of rebukes, and the wicked daughter of the devil feared the severed head of the just man; and so, deceived by the perversity of her thoughts, she believed she would thereafter remain hidden. So the monks, who had been held worthy of so great a revelation from Christ's forerunner, took up the venerable head and hastened to return home. Now at the same time a certain potter of the city of Emesa, oppressed by many hardships and lacking all necessities, since he could no longer struggle against extreme poverty, was overcome with great weariness because of the hardship of his want, and believed he would preserve his life by going away. It happened to him as he fled that he met these monks, who were carrying the most precious vessel of the desert. And when he became their companion and fellow traveller, they entrusted the burden to him as to a faithful man, as travellers commonly do with one another, and explained the vision that had been revealed to them. But to the potter, who did not know the mystery, the forerunner appeared and warned him to slip away from his companions and to take what he was carrying and flee. When he had done this, he returned to his own house, from which he had departed; and from that time he continued flourishing in every kind of prosperity. He understood who was the author of his prosperity, and offered him honour with devoted zeal, as befitted his means. When he saw death approaching, he carefully sealed the water-jar in which he kept that gift enclosed and entrusted it to his own sister, telling her of his former want and revealing the wealth that was now in his hands. And when he had told her of the miseries of his first poverty, from which he had to flee, and had shown the way in which he had been rescued from them, he begged her to treat the deposit with honour and not to open the jar before the outcome of events should show what was inside. He was thinking, as I suppose, that the vessel was like a womb for the forerunner, so that, just as when placed in his mother's womb he had made the Lord known, so surely, living after death, he would reveal the mystery of that urn at the fitting time. And therefore he did not keep silent about the author of his unhoped-for change [another reading: the author of his change inspiring him], but said: "O woman, you will learn by experience itself, and you will come to know our manner of life and conduct since we were found worthy to possess this treasure. If therefore you too hold it in reverence, you will enjoy an abundance of all good things, present as well as future. But if perhaps length of time takes away your strength, or violent sickness of body wears you down, so that you cannot pay the zeal that is owed, do not delay to hand this gift over to some pious and faithful man." After her brother's death, as long as she had strength equal to her devotion, she is shown to have loved the holy charge. But when she yielded to the necessity of old age, she made known what her brother had enjoined on her, and handed it over to those who were to receive the pious deposit. And when very many had received this gift in succession one after another, a certain Eustathius, a monk by name and a priest of another sect, also received what was kept in the jar, sealed as it was. Surely those who gave it could not discern his religion and judged him a pious man. He, very cunningly ascribing to himself the cures that were conferred on those who came by the power of the holy head, tried like a most wicked tavern-keeper to adulterate the truth of the faith. At last, having become known to those servants [of God] who glorified the blessed Trinity rightly, holily and inseparably, he, who under the pretext of veneration of the Father is shown to have been insulting to Christ the Son of God by diminishing him, began to be expelled from the city of Emesa, with the judges also cooperating. He begged those who were seeking, for their salvation, to separate him from the holy flock and drive him away, to grant him the space of at least a single day to stay in the cave in which the holy [deposit] was known to have been placed, since he was also already pressed by the closeness of night. But by God's providence he was cheated of his hope. For he could not obtain [his request], so that what he was scheming was not accomplished. So venerable men, following the way of the solitary life, took over that same cave. And after many had succeeded one another in the monastery, at last, under the archimandrite Marcellus, divine grace deigned to reveal him whose birth Gabriel announced and whom a barren mother bore: the dweller in the desert, the greatest rebuker of impiety and avenger of the law, the forerunner of the Lord, the friend of the Bridegroom, the Saviour's Baptist, the herald of truth and most fervent lover of justice. The aforesaid venerable archimandrite Marcellus related the manner of this appearance in these words.
On the second finding of the precious head of the holy and illustrious prophet, the forerunner John the Baptist. By the same translator.

There appeared, he says, the thrice most blessed and universal apostle and faithful friend of our Saviour Jesus Christ, in the middle of a week of the forty days of the holy fasts, on the eighteenth day of the month Peritius, that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, in the seven hundred and sixty-third year, in the sixth indiction, in the reign of Valentinian and Marcian, most pious emperors and servants of God, under Uranius, most holy bishop of the city of Emesa, to whom this same thing was also revealed on the twenty-fourth day of the same month, that is, the sixth day before the Kalends of March. And he revealed [it] to me, Marcellus, who was in great fear and reverence, in the form of a fiery star, according to the most trustworthy visions set out below: he who founded all things in his power and prepared [them] in his wisdom; who knows all things before they come to be, and orders everything for the salvation of the human race; who is blessed above all for ever. Amen. So God deigned to make me, his servant, the beholder of the vision set forth. For I saw in a vision of the night, and behold, the doors of our monastery were open, and, seized with great fear, I ran to shut them. And again I see a river bursting out at our doors. When I had seen this, I wondered in amazement where so vast a mass of water came from. And while I was turning this over within myself, raising my eyes I saw Marcellus the presbyter, who was second after Maxentius the archimandrite, coming from the southern side of the river, and we heard the voices of many companies from the eastern quarter of the basilica of the holy martyr Julian. A great sound of them was carried to us, and the peoples were hurrying through the waters themselves with eager rush. And as I marvelled how, walking in the midst of the waters, they came swiftly to us, and how each company chanted psalms in its own tongue, suddenly a voice was heard of those who were crying out from the east: 'Behold, Saint John the Baptist is coming down.' And while I was standing at the southern door, the eastern gates were opened, and the companies of psalm-singers came straight in. So leaving the sight of the river, and standing at the foot of the stairs, I watched their holy office, which they were celebrating in the monastery. And standing on the same stairs, I saw two courts, one facing west and the other south; and between the two courts a great temple, and each company entered the court that faced east, and worshipped toward the temple. But entering the southern court, they at once fell quiet. And when the companies had fallen silent, others went ahead and cried out: 'Behold, Saint John is coming.' And while I was standing at the same place on the stairs, Saint John, the forerunner of the Lord, came, and I saw him in the temple that had been shown to me; and behold, there was one at his right and one at his left. And as he stood in the temple, the peoples of the companies began to approach him one after another and to be blessed by him; and likewise, chanting psalms, they set off for the basilica of the holy martyr Stephen. And when the companies had passed through, I too thought to go to him, to be blessed by him. And it seemed good to me to go in by those doors by which the companies had entered. And since I had not seen that they gave anyone the kiss of peace, but only that they kissed his feet, approaching him from the front with fear and reverence, I ran with my head bowed to the ground and held his feet. But he took hold of my chin and kissed me. When I had been granted this, I at once awoke. And after a few days had passed, I see, and behold, the doors of the monastery on the southern side were open again, and I was shouting, as it were, at the brothers why they had left those doors [open]; and I went with quick step to shut them, and behold, I see Saint John standing at the outer door, and with him those two whom I had seen before, and I went up to be blessed by him, and raising me up again, he gave me peace. His garments were white; and presently drawing from his bosom a vessel full of honey, he gave [it] to me, saying: 'Receive this blessing,' and he poured that vessel of honey over my hands, and I asked him, saying: 'Lord Saint John, where have you come to us from?' He answered: 'I have come from Sebaste.' So I went before him, and both he and those who were with him entered our monastery, and again he poured the vessel of honey over my hands. And when I had carried his blessing to the upper part of the dining-hall, he entered the oratory; and when I had gone down to the oratory where he was, behold, I see a pillar of fire before him. And seized with great dread, I was woken. After this, before the door of the monastery where the holy deposit was had been handed over to us, in the holy days of the fasts, when we had taken food in the evening, I said to our brothers, 'Let none of you neglect to repeat his psalms.' And leaving me in the dining-hall, they went down to the foot of the stairs that looks toward both monasteries. And when they had sat down to repeat the psalms, Brother Isaac, raising his eyes to the right, saw fire burning on the panels of the door of the cave where the venerable head of Saint John the Baptist had been laid away. When the brother saw this, he cried out and said: 'My lord, my lord, a fire has been kindled at the door of the cave.' And I answered: 'Do not be afraid, brother, but, guarding yourself with the sign of Christ, stay right there.' But the brothers, shutting the door out of fear, came hurrying to me. I, however, recognising the mystery from the visions shown to me before, said to them: 'Do not be afraid, my brothers, for the Lord will make this turn out well for us.' And after five days Maxentius and Stephen, venerable presbyters and archimandrites, coming to the holy bishop on the Lord's day in the evening, put to him everything about that cave, which adjoined our monastery, so that both might be joined together; and the bishop ordered this to be done. The presbyter Stephen said to him: 'By our order I will hand the cave over to Brother Marcellus early tomorrow.' And arriving in the morning he handed that monastery over to us in the presence of the presbyters Palladius, Peter, Gennadius, and Stephen, archimandrite of the monastery of the Bethgali. And opening the door that was barred, we went in together and worshipped. And seeing that the place was very much neglected, he urged us to take care of it. And that same presbyter Stephen set out to visit the monasteries that were situated in the hamlets. I, Marcellus, taking the brothers, began to devote care to the monastery that had been given to us. And while we were cleaning those places, Peter, presbyter of the place Bethmamas, came and said to me: 'Stephen, archimandrite of the Bethgali, begs that for the Lord's sake you come with us to the monastery of blessed Carterius.' And I answered that I could not come, because I was devoting care to the place entrusted to me; but he compelled me to set out with him. And as we were going along together, I say to him: 'Let us go up and greet Cyriacus, deacon and archimandrite.' And going up and greeting him, we began to want to go on to the aforesaid monastery of blessed Carterius. And the deacon Cyriacus said to me: 'Did you come for this, to leave without delay?' I answered him: 'We must travel quickly, because another monastery has also been handed over to us by the bishop, to which we are urgently devoting care.' So going down we came to the monastery often mentioned; and when we had greeted the brothers and arranged what was necessary, we were returning. The aforesaid Peter and Stephen, presbyters and archimandrites, say to me: 'We bid you farewell; pray for us.' Then I say to them: 'Today we have taken over the monastery, and you want to go away? Stay, I beg you, and comfort us'; and I prevailed on them. And when evening had come, after prayers, having taken food, we went to rest: both of them in the upper dining-hall, I there in the inner chamber.

And as I was sleeping on that night on which the door of the monastery, or of the cave, was opened, that is, on the following day, the third day of the week, after the night prayers, something like a man's hand struck me three times on the right side, and I heard a great voice saying to me: 'Behold, the door is open, and therefore recognise him who has made an entrance for you, lest you perhaps neglect [it].' And I, with great fear, turned and sat up, and I see a flaming star at the door where I was resting. And seized with greater fear, I signed myself with the cross of Christ, and it did not move from that place at all. So I got up and put my hands on the door where it was, and again it was found at the next door. When I had opened the door, one of those who were resting there noticed. And when I had come to the second door, the star was found at the third door. Then I see it on the inner steps of the stairs. And the doors of both monasteries were likewise open, and the door of the cave lay open. And behold, the star itself went before me, and I, following it, went in until it stopped in the little apse of the cave; and seeing this miracle, I worshipped the Lord, prostrate on the ground, for many hours. But I remembered that I had as guests the venerable men Peter and Stephen, presbyters and archimandrites, and so that they should not suspect where I had been in the night, I rose from prayer. And going up again, when I wanted to enter the chamber, they say to me: 'Where have you been so long?' I answered: 'I went down for a necessary need.' And when I wanted to go in where I had been resting, they say to me: 'Are you going in again?' But I, feeling that I had been made dazed by the revelation I had seen, asked pardon as one unwell, and at once withdrew. And after morning had come, bidding me farewell, they went off to their own cells. And when they had set out at dawn, I instructed the brothers who were with me: 'Shut the gates, staying outside, and if perhaps anyone comes to look for me, say that I am busy.' For the presbyter Palladius often came, going in and reading the Gospel. So when he had come as usual, the brothers then refused him entry, stating what was true, that the Gospel too was under the archimandrite's key, and excuses were made to him. He came a second time too, and came a third, and so he entered. For I, taking a censer, put incense in it, and humbly besought the gracious Lord to show me the place of the heavenly treasure. Taking also a mattock, I began to dig, and came to a place that was built of lime and ordinary tiles. And the further I went down in digging, the louder a sound was given back, as if from the striking of a water-jar.

And after I had dug and gone down as far as the floor, I found what looked like sand cast from bronze, and with much labour I was barely able to separate out the sand. After this, when the sand had been removed, a larger tile appeared. Lifting this, I found beneath it a marble slab; and lifting the slab, I found a water-jar. Lighting a lamp with fear and reverence, and putting incense in the censer, I felt this [jar] carefully, and worshipping the Lord I remained dazed for a long while, and covered the holy water-jar again. But at once the deacon and archimandrite Gennadius came to us, and greeting me at the entrance of the cave he said to me: 'Come, I pray, let us go into the cave together.' And after we had worshipped there, he gave me the kiss of peace, and my brothers too, and said: 'I have just come from my monastery of Caperelum, and I saw this dream. It was as though we both stood in a certain cave, in which there was a great quantity of the purest loaves, like the sun, and a portion laid on top of the loaves. And an immense [multitude] of people kept coming and taking from them. And they did not run out, nor did the people who had received cease [coming]. And when we were now failing because of the size of the crowds, the loaves began to fly up over our hands, and so all received, as many as streamed together to this grace of a gift.' And after he had told me the dream, I answered: 'What you have seen is good.' And pondering within myself what this vision meant, and going over again the things that had gone before, I said that this vision was from God. And knowing that these things had happened by divine will, I made known how holy John the Baptist had deigned to appear; and as soon as he heard, he remained dazed, and began to beg me to show him the place, which I also did. After this we both went out, and discussed what ought to be done, and it seemed good to me that I should go first and inform Stephen, presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery called Claramnium, and that through him he should make it known to the bishop. And coming to his monastery, we did not find him. For he had gone away, as we said, to the monasteries that were in the countryside, on the very day on which he had given us the monastery and opened the entrance of the cave. And when we had gone out, we decided to call Cyriacus, deacon and archimandrite, to us, and reveal to him the mystery by which holy John had deigned to appear to us. So we sent brother Isaac to him, saying: 'Come to us quickly.' And when the brother had come to him and told him, he came at once in obedience. And when we had greeted him, he told us a dream that he had seen, and it agreed with the vision that the deacon Gennadius had related to me. And when we had prayed, we at once took care to make known to him the revelation of holy John the Baptist, and he said: 'Let us consider what ought to be done.' And I said: 'I think it fitting that we make this known to the bishop.' And learning again that the often-mentioned Stephen, presbyter and archimandrite, had not come back from the country, we waited five days after the revelation had been shown to us. But on the sabbath day, in the afternoon, as we were sitting and talking, Saltus the collector and Maris the linen-seller, a litter-bearer, came in to us, and having spoken with us they at once withdrew. And I told brother Isaac to shut the door behind them. And again as we sat and talked, I was suddenly struck in the knees, so that I was bent right over and could not get up at all or do any work. Then Gennadius and Cyriacus, deacons and archimandrites, say to me: 'Did we not tell you: Do not make delays, but let us go and bring it to the bishop's notice, since the presbyter Stephen is said not yet to have come back?' And I remained grievously afflicted. They, however, having celebrated the evening office, came in where I was lying, and declared, saying: 'We have given satisfaction to holy John by an oath, taking your part, that tomorrow before sunrise the bishop will learn the whole matter through you.' And I answered: 'You have done very well in promising this very thing'; and at once I was relieved of the pains. And on the following day, the Lord's day, coming together with the deacon Cyriacus and the monk Julian, we informed the bishop as he was then coming out of the church after the morning prayers, saying that holy John the Baptist had been revealed. He, astounded, said: 'No one has known of this; and which of you would dare to touch it?' And the deacon Cyriacus said to him: 'When will you deign to come?' And he said: 'I will come tomorrow.' And on the next day the bishop came with presbyters and deacons, and going into the place they fell on their faces and worshipped. But the presbyter Malchus, one of those who had come with the bishop, moved by unbelief, said: 'How is it certain that this is the head of the forerunner?' And putting out his hand to touch the water-jar, at once it withered, and his hand stuck to the water-jar, and he could not draw it away. But when prayer had been made urgently by all, and all were glorifying God and praying for him, at last he was barely able to draw his hand away, but it remained powerless. Then the bishop, with all who were with him, taking up the water-jar with the holy treasure laid in it, placed it for the time in the diaconicon, that is, in the sacristy of the church, until a basilica should be built in his name. When this was completed, and the day of his holy deposition was at hand, holy John appeared to the man whose hand had withered, saying: 'In the procession itself, when the deposition takes place, put your hand on the water-jar, and at once it will be healed.' And when he had done this, it was restored to its former health. The deposition of St John the Forerunner and Baptist took place in his church on the twenty-sixth of the month of October, in the year 763, in the sixth indiction, in the reign of the religious, pious and orthodox Augusti Valentinian the Younger and Marcian, princes worthy of everlasting memory: to the praise and glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory with the undefiled Father and the most holy and life-giving Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.
A sermon on the first, second and third finding of the precious head of St John the Baptist, the forerunner. Translated by the Reverend Father Combefis.

Again the divine forerunner has come to us, and again a speech comes forward to hold a festal gathering, and to celebrate thanksgiving before the assembly collected here. Many are the feasts of the admirable herald, all alike splendid and illustrious; and anyone can take from each one a distinguished theme for himself, so that each may contribute what he can, and one may commemorate one [feast], another another, since even to commemorate just one, and to praise it as it deserves, is not merely difficult for speech but impossible. For not only does the forerunner's birth surpass thought and the power of speech, but also that earlier conception and the leaping in his mother's womb, which prophecy also followed. Besides, there is also his upbringing, to which none of other men's is like. The coming of so great a man to the Jordan, too: what power of speech would it not surpass and drive into straits? And what would you say of the Lord's coming to him, his head bowed to him, the touch of the hand, and the hidden cleansing of baptism?

For all these I have a separate and proper feast, together also with the glorious beheading which the greatest of men endured, struck on the head by Herod as the wages of a wanton and shameless dance. But since this is not the time to commemorate these things, as they also have their own days assigned, and they have been related by us briefly above: leaving them aside, if you please, we shall turn the discourse to other things, which we have also resolved to treat at present. Plainly the aim set for this speech is to describe the finding of the precious head; that is, its disclosure and bringing forth into the open. For we know that this [finding] was not one only, but also a second and a third. Since, then, by the hidden counsel of God it has been hidden three times already, and as many times has come forth and emerged from the bosom of the earth, it will be worth the effort, after mentioning first the first and then the second finding, to pass from there in order to the third; which the present speech also has as its theme; although otherwise it is fitting that it should also cleave to the others, and not depend singly on any one, as one that makes use of them all. In this way, then, let it take up the matter and show its purpose, for the sake of which it was composed, since it plainly falls short in other titles. And from here its narrative must begin.

Now, then, the admirable John, great herald and forerunner of the Truth, had been beheaded by Herod; and Herodias, after the shameless dance, had placed [the head] safely in dark recesses in the palace itself. For the wicked woman feared that, joined to the rest of the trunk, he would be raised again to convict her crime. Yet she did not receive the wages of what she had done postponed for long, since she herself ended her life by a most shameful fate, and after her her daughter too; for her neck was cut by the ice of a river in winter, so that an equal punishment might meet the offence. So, then, John's head having been cut off, as we said, and laid away in this manner by the shameless woman in a hiding-place in the earth, that precious and most beneficial jewel remained for many years unseen by the people, untouched, unapproachable: so perhaps the divine herald providently arranged it, lest from its easy possession its loss too should come easily to us, and the longing for it be despised; and otherwise also, while the persecution from idol-worship was growing strong under the authority of Diocletian and Maximian, it was not fitting that the noble treasure should be disclosed to a vile race of men and thrown to swine, since it was more illustrious than any pearl. For this reason, I think, the sacred head remained hidden, so as to be unknown to the people, and did not disclose itself. But if there is some other, more hidden reason why it was concealed and delayed its finding, let those know it who behold greater things and apply their mind to loftier matters.

When the time was now approaching at which it was to be uncovered and brought out of its hiding-place in the earth, then it is indeed uncovered and brought out of hiding, at the time and in the manner that pleased him who was being brought out. As for the time, the epoch was when Constantine the Great had taken up the sceptre of the empire. As for the manner, let us see in what manner, and by whose agency, it was made manifest and came to this first finding.

Two monks set out from the East and came to Jerusalem, eager to see the Lord's sepulchre and to visit all the holy places there. The divine forerunner appeared to one of them and said: "Go, both of you, to the royal house of Herod, and take up my head, which is buried under the earth in that place." When he told his brother the vision, and the other refused to believe it, and both delayed to go where they had been ordered, John again presented himself to both, gave the same orders, and sharpened their desire. They set out at once, full of confidence, since the forerunner himself, as it seemed to them, was making their way easy. They immediately dug up the place and brought out the head, which glowed as if with a gleam of light and breathed out a fragrance of the sweetest scent, beyond explaining in any words. They put the head into a sack of goat's hair (so, I think, it seemed good to the Baptist, since he himself covered his body with camel's hair), and went away from there. While they were on their way, a potter fell in with them, a man struggling with extreme poverty and in utterly wretched circumstances. When he had met them and, as happens, joined them as a companion on the road, he became a companion of their burden too, ordered by them to carry the sack. Foolish and fickle men, to hand over their good and their treasure to another! The poor man carried it, though the treasure entrusted to him was unknown to him, for the monks had not told him. But the divine forerunner appeared to him, since it seemed to him quite fitting that the gift should fall to this man, and both taught him what he was secretly carrying and ordered him to flee with it. Unknown to his companions he fled with all speed, carrying off the treasure in safety; and it brought him countless good things from then on, so that he was strong in wealth, enjoyed prosperity, and all else turned out well for him. When he was about to depart from human life, he handed the gift, safely placed in a small chest, to his sister, and warned her not to take it out of the chest before [someone] announced the end of her life: for truly this was something great, and would provide great things. "For to us too," he said, "it has brought great blessings, such that one could not easily match them in words. You too will at once be made a sharer in them, provided you hold the pledge in honour and venerate it; and when you are about to leave human life, you will hand it as a deposit to one of the faithful, and leave it by will to someone dear [to you] for his upright character." When he had given his sister these instructions, he departed from life; and she, as was fitting, greatly rejoicing at the gift and devoted to it in her heart, venerated it just as her brother had, and she too was enriched with many benefits from it. When her life too was declining to its close, she consigned the treasure as a deposit to companions, and with many words warned and begged them to guard it carefully.

After many others in succession had in turn held the pledge, and the deposit had passed from some to others, it finally came into the hands of a certain monk. Eustathius was his name; but his mind was in no way sound in the faith, although his error had escaped others. He too, trafficking in grace, both concealed the pledge entrusted to him and, with it, the opinion he held (he was, that is, an Arian). But when the people of Emesa, from where he also came, at last recognised the man's character and faith and were about to drive him from the city, he asked for a respite of even a single day, and then they might expel him. This was a malicious scheme, full of cunning. For he had laid the sacred head in a certain cave and put it in a water-jar, with a stone covering placed over the mouth and sand heaped on it; and for this reason he was angling for that delay, so that he might take the pledge away from there and, madman that he was, make it his own property. But the people of Emesa, not allowing him to stay even a moment, sent him off at once, since the divine man plainly sharpened their impulse and drove them to perform this good deed without delay. After this, monks succeeded [to the place] in the cave, men pursuing the best kind of life; they lived in the place, yet in no way knew the pledge hidden in it, that most abundant treasure. And in this way the first finding itself was completed, carried out on this very day, about the twenty-fourth of February, as is conjectured.

But since, as they say, it happened that the pledge was hidden again, namely when the Eustathius just mentioned had made his scheme out of depravity of mind, it is worth the effort for us to say in what manner, at what time, and by whose agency the venerable head was found a second time too, so that we may pass to the third finding, for whose sake our speech was composed.

A certain Marcellus, distinguished in life and devout in character, who was also head of the monastery situated by the cave, one night in the middle week of the fasts saw a dream of this kind, and told the vision to the brothers who served under him, in roughly these words: "It seemed to me," he said, "that all the doors of the monastery were open, and through them a river was passing with a great roar and rush of waters." Struck with amazement at this, he turned the vision over within himself, not knowing what to conjecture or what the sight pointed to. "And indeed," he said, "while I was in this state, at once a voice was borne from on high, with a dreadful and great sound. Then too a harmony of people singing psalms sweetly was heard. Those who performed this office were distributed separately into companies. The sense of the voice was this: 'Behold, the great John, the Baptist of Christ, is being shown.' The companies that sent forth this voice entered, each in turn, by the eastern gate.

"While I, amazed at what had appeared, was leaning on a ladder placed there, I see again two courts: one stretched out to the east, the other to the south. In the middle stood a most beautiful church, and the companies, entering it one by one, reverently performed adoration. Then also two others of outstanding appearance became visible to me at once, and cried out in these words: 'See, here is the great John in the church; see him and believe.' And I saw him shining with great brightness. He looked at the companies entering with smiling eyes, and bestowed on each in order the gift of a blessing. When those blessings had been imparted and come to their end, I too approached to be given a blessing by him. And I fell at his feet, all trembling and afraid. But he at once raised me up and, filling me with confidence, kindly nodded [to me] to kiss his awesome mouth. Then also, bringing out from his bosom a vessel full of honey, he handed it into my hands and bade me take it. As soon as I had taken it, I went out from there, and acted as guide on the way. Then he followed behind me without delay, and together we both entered the monastery. The companies I had seen were his companions, and with them I also saw a pillar of fire shining before them. At this, struck with greater fear, I shook off sleep in my agitation. Such was what befell me in a dream, a long one, needing a long explanation, no less dreadful than true, since both qualities are found in it. Meanwhile, remaining in doubt, I order those under me each to perform the customary portion of prayers twice over. Among them one, named Isaac, while still singing psalms and lifting his eyes to God, sees a burning fire before the cave, rushing within the doors of the church. He at once showed the sight. I, bidding him keep silent, since from the earlier vision I had received a sense of the matter beforehand, freed him from fear; for he seemed to me to have been terrified. After another five days had passed, another vision again came to me.

"For a hand appearing by night struck my right thigh, and from it also a voice resounded, crying in these words: 'Rise; see, I am granted to you as a gift. Moreover a star will also meet you, which will show the place.' Then I rose at once, and at the same time the star went before, until it came and stood above the place where the cave was, in which there was also an adjoining niche, under which the sacred pledge had been buried. So when I had seen so clear a sign, falling on my knees and making many supplications to him who had made himself visible to me, I began to dig the place with a mattock. Then, reaching deep and coming upon some sand poured in, after which there was also a tile, then a stone covering, beneath it I found the most precious pledge, covered by a water-jar and stored in it. Made glad in heart at this, I at once covered the place again, taking nothing out from there, and so far revealing to no one what had been seen.

"But since shortly afterwards Abbot Gennadius also came to us, a man who had obtained from God the gift of immense grace, and who himself had seen a vision akin to the vision made to me related a little above, which he also set out to me in full, point by point, I too, setting aside all hesitation, revealed to him what had been shown to me, telling each thing word for word and hiding nothing from him. Then he, seized with joy and amazement, asked that both the pit and the place be shown him, and where the sacred pledge had been laid. And indeed I show [them], and do not keep so great a man from the sight.

"When, therefore, we had parted from each other, I was again tossed on a sea of thoughts, turning over in my mind what I ought to do. Then this great [thought] also seemed to be offered to me: that I should confer about the matter with the bishop (Uranius was at that time in charge of the Church of the Emesenes), and should both take him as a helper in what had appeared and make use of his counsels in the matter. But since I did not carry the matter out at once, and delayed the undertaking, with my thoughts pulling me this way and that, and referring it to others, namely Cyriacus the deacon and certain others, I then also came to feel [the fault] of an ill-advised mind, and how much evil the delay brought me. For on the evening of the Sabbath, while I was sitting with those who were present and talking of some things, suddenly someone dealt a blow to my knees, and rendered the whole [of me] motionless, scarcely able to bend to the ground. When they saw this, those who were present, and above all Gennadius whom I mentioned, turned to prayers and vows, and asked the great forerunner to free me from the mishap and restore my feet sound as before. For they knew on what account I had been so punished, and that the cause was the matter I had neglected and my delay.

"When, as soon as the vow was made, I had recovered feet fit for walking, I at once went with those companions to the bishop, judging that no business should be put before this. Then I revealed everything that had been seen to him too: the dream, the vision, the cave, the place, the buried water-jar, and finally the sacred head, on whose account all these things [had happened]. The bishop at once girded himself for the matter, and gladly obeyed the command; and so, as the Lord's day was dawning, he came to the place with lamps, and reverently and with fear, stretching out his hand to the water-jar, he brought out the head, a dreadful sight to those who saw it, and, except to them, incredible to others. For hairs seemed to have grown on it, a sweet scent breathed from it, and an indescribable brightness flashed out.

Now since a presbyter accompanying the bishop, named [Mal]chus, was half in doubt and hesitated whether this was the head of the forerunner, putting his hand to it too boldly (since that wicked one is wont to envy the good), he too at once reaped the fruit of unbelief, his right hand withering and clinging to the urn to which he had put it. And indeed he would have remained so, had not those present for many hours besought the saint to heal him who was guilty, and to be reconciled to him who had doubted. The head of the forerunner having then been taken up (namely on 24 February, on which day the first finding had also taken place), Bishop Uranius laid the precious pledge for the time being in his own church; and shortly afterwards, raising a church to the Baptist as well, when much labour had been put into it, he transferred the gift there, for the city of Emesa, and a rich and inexhaustible treasure for every other city and region. So far the second finding and manifestation, made at the time when Valentinian and Marcian held the sceptres of empire. But it is worth while that we should also relate the one that happened recently, the third, for whose sake also this discourse was undertaken by us, which is also better known and more illustrious than the others.

So when the sacred head had been laid up at Emesa, as we have said, and was offering the richest gift of grace to those who came from nearby and from far off and from every side, the treasure remained for many years bound to that place: and although it was confined there, yet its powers were not restricted by its bounds, but it spread out its benefits abundantly, so that they reached all. But how hidden are God's purposes, and how incomprehensible his judgements! For when he had allowed the region of Emesa and the city of Emesa itself to be taken by the hands of barbarians and to come under their rule, he did not, however, think it right that the most precious head too should be in their possession and bound to them. And so it was not, but, taken from there by the work of a certain pious and honourable worshipper, it was then transferred elsewhere: namely to Comana, a small and obscure city, which, however, enriched by that pledge, became illustrious and was thereafter more famous than the rest.

The vessel which had and held the treasure within was a silver urn fitted with gold plates, so that the precious pledge might be kept in a precious vessel. But most people did not know, and especially the citizens of the queen of cities, in what place it had been laid: both because the translation had been made secretly and without witness, and because the time at which it had taken place was not known. For no one, as far as we have been able to find out, openly recorded the matter. So the head remained at Comana, not well known, I think, even to the inhabitants themselves. For both the times and deep affairs had covered the matter with ignorance; especially since the Iconoclasts had meanwhile arisen, who were so far from paying honour to the relics of the saints that wherever these were known to exist, they gave them to the flames. For that reason, then, the most sacred pledge was thereafter visible or known to no one. But after the supreme power returned to the orthodox, and the sceptres were again entrusted to faithful emperors, and the impious Iconoclasts perished with a crash, meeting, that is, with fitting punishment, then indeed it pleased the forerunner too to make his head manifest; and to hand over the astonishing gift not to this or that city (small towns, namely, bounded by small limits), but to the greatest and most royal of all, namely Constantinople; so that the treasure might be kept inviolate, and the city honoured by its deposition, and so that the sacred gift itself, as is fitting, might borrow some splendour from it, since in its keeping it would have greater honours and more lavish worship. For at that time Michael and Theodora had taken up the sceptres, and Ignatius, successor of Methodius, a man famous for many virtues, was governing the Church. Under these illustrious [rulers] this most precious pledge too was brought into the queen of cities, and obtained this third and last finding. Now the manner of the finding was as follows.

One night, while the pontiff, who shared his name and was akin in character to the famous Theophorus, was offering praises to God, a divine vision from heaven came to him (namely that the city of Comana had the most precious head, enclosed in a silver urn and laid in a sacred place; and that it was worth while that it be transferred to Byzantium; for so it seemed good to the forerunner too). He also declared to the emperor what had been seen. Both, then, being well disposed to the matter, men were at once sent by each to take up the treasure. When these had come to the place and had learned where the head had been laid, by the sign the pontiff had indicated to them, they reverently drew it out from there. Indeed, before sure news of the matter had yet been brought to the city, the emperor together with the patriarch, and all the nobles at court, all the clergy and monks, poured out of the city and went to meet it with incense and lamps, and escorted the head with much ceremony in procession; and they put to it their eyes, and lips, and brows, and above all their breasts. Then the pontiff, lifting it up with trembling hand, brought the treasure into the palace church and laid it there: namely on the 25th day of the month of May. For this is the day of the celebration, the feast, that is, of the third Finding or Deposition. For it may be called either, since one solemnity is held under the name of both. For it was fitting that a worshipper of the Trinity, and one who had clearly revealed its mystery to others, should also give up his head to be found three times, neither falling short of that number nor exceeding it; so that in this way too, as in others, he might be united to the first and leading Trinity and be honoured with its number. For it is a precious number, and worthy, so to speak, of all acceptance. For there are three whom we worship, thus distinct in persons, though they are united in nature. Likewise three parts are recognised in the soul, by which the rational animal is moved and driven; three dimensions too in the body, by which it is defined; three laws given to man, by which he might be ordered: natural, written, and of grace. By three contemplations the mind lifts up its desire: namely natural, intelligible, and that which exceeds every power of the intellect. For it has nowhere further to reach, even if it be most keen-sighted. There are three immersions in baptism, too, which also figure and darkly signify the Trinity. Threefold was the breathing of the Holy Spirit made by the Saviour upon the disciples, by which they obtained an abundant gift of grace. Likewise there are three changes of things, which they call earthquakes, although one of these has not yet occurred. But what need is there to say more about the number three and the Trinity? For as the Trinity is the head of our faith, so plainly the number three too is outstanding among numbers, and this finding of the sacred pledge is counted along with it, and has thereby gained greater honour. For it is not one and single, since one is an imperfect number and lacks quantity; nor twofold, since the number two is mixed with matter, from which John was pure. So for that reason it is threefold, because the number three is held in honour by him and is dear to him, as being, of course, honoured by the Trinity and counted with it.

But since we know you, most blessed forerunner, to be a worshipper of the Trinity and its best herald, for whose sake also your neck was cut, do not cease to make it gracious to us; so that, among other things, we may walk the path that leads to it, avoiding under your guidance whatever is crooked, and directed onto straight ways. For your lavish love and affection towards us is not hidden from us, nor how daily you impart rich grace to us, since you preside over your flock, and as a generous rewarder bestow great gifts on those who are constant in your church: which may we too obtain, and departing hence be set before the holy Trinity and be illumined by its light, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong honour and worship with the unbegotten Father and the most holy Spirit, now and for ages of ages. Amen.
Praise by our holy father and confessor Theodore the Studite on the third finding of the venerable head of the most holy forerunner.
(From manuscript codex of the Royal Library no. 273. It also survives in two other Royal codices.)

Today's day, most devout hearers, bringing a third announcement for the memory of the forerunner, gathers us together. For if, when a treasure is found by chance, everyone runs together with joy and seeks to see the thing longed for, what delight of a festal day does it not rightly demand that now the supremely venerable head of the Baptist, far more precious than all gold and precious stones, has been revealed by the gracious will of God, who arranges all things for the salvation of the human race?

Let us then exult in it and rejoice, since for men of devout mind the receiving of spiritual gifts is exultation. Let us sing in gladness; let us praise in thanksgiving: this is another solemnity, another praise. The feast of his nativity shows the likeness of a rising; for it presents the spiritual morning star in such a way that he rises wondrously for the world from his mother's womb. That of his beheading shows a setting; for it represents the same divine luminary in such a way that, having completed the course of the whole spiritual day, he goes down beneath the earth, and there scatters upon those placed in the underworld the gleams that go before the coming of Christ. Finally, the day we now keep hints at something more hidden, namely the resurrection of eternal life. For the forerunner has risen and, as it were, been restored to life again by the showing of his most sacred head. O wondrous thing! The earth did not bear to keep this treasure within itself for longer years and to afflict us with its loss; but at a proper time of its own it brings forth its fruit, like a new and ripe fruit. So heaven saw the sacred head and rejoiced; the human race beheld it and poured itself out in praises; the demons perceived it and burst asunder. It shone more brightly than the sun with the light of truth, more brilliantly than the moon with the radiance of piety; it surpasses the variety of the stars with the multitude of its miracles. For what streams of cures, and how great, at once flowed from it, clearer and more abundant than any spring? Soon it breathed forth the grace of the Spirit, more fragrant and more potent than all the lilies of the field. The whole world smelled the sweetest odour and exulted. All drew from it, and took for themselves what they sought and as much as they desired, according as they were moved in their hearts. For the grace is most abundant, so that as much is received as the set will of a faithful mind has overflowed. 'The head of their circuit' (namely of sinners), says David, 'the labour of their own lips' (Ps. 139:10); but for us this head has emerged as the release from labours, the driving off of diseases, the flight of demons, the generous bestowal of every divine gift. For it is the head of him who leapt in exultation in the womb of a barren woman, because of the presence of God the Word incarnate in the womb of a virgin, of whom the most sacred David says: 'Man shall come forth, and a lofty heart; and God shall be exalted' (Ps. 63:8). It is the head of him who was filled with the Holy Spirit even from the womb, of whom the great Zachariah says: 'And you, child, shall be called prophet of the Most High: for you shall go before the Lord, to prepare his ways' (Luke 1:76). It is the head of him who from the very cradle until his showing to Israel undertook to live in the desert, of whom the prophet Isaiah says: 'The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight' (Isa. 40:3). It is the head of him who preached a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins; of whom Scripture speaks thus: 'Behold, I send my angel before you' (Mal. 3:1).

But what need is there to say more? It is the head of him who was found worthy to touch the divine crown, to whom the Lord says: 'Let it be so now; for thus it befits us to fulfil all righteousness' (Matt. 3:15). But how could any mortal at all praise the most blessed head as befits it? What tongue of the earth-born could celebrate sufficiently that head, wholly admirable and radiant with the gleams of incorruption?

But, O divine and sacred head, little vessel of the most sincere and pure senses! spiritual censer of the fragrance of the sweet Spirit! richest storehouse of the wonders of rich grace! I praise your divinely braided locks, more precious than the gold of Ophir, surpassing in beauty the headbands of brides, over which the razor of vice (the deception of sin, that is) did not pass, as once it did over Samson when Delilah raged against him. I magnificently proclaim your sacred beard, surpassing Aaron's (Ps. 132:2), from which the dew of health flowed into the souls of the faithful, better than the dew of Hermon which descends on the mountains of Zion. I venerate your shining eyes, most splendid torches of the Spirit, purer than the eyes of a dove, and more precious than the most precious emeralds. Your ears, inspired by God, instruments fitted for heavenly voices, I offer with praises. I shall fittingly apply to you, in a moral sense, these words of Scripture: How beautiful are those cheeks, like a turtle-dove's (Song 1:9 and 4:3), as it is in the Song: 'Like the rind of a pomegranate are your cheeks; like a scarlet thread your lips; like the tower of Lebanon your nose, and your speech sweet and comely' (Song 7:4 and 4:3). I praise the fence of your teeth, gleaming with the whiteness of milk, from which went forth the word of divine preaching to the ends of the world. Finally I praise your neck, whiter than silver, which the most wicked sword pierced, and from which, instead of blood, fountains of miracles flowed.

What do you say, Herod? For now I must turn my speech to you. Did you obtain what you sought? Did you gain what you desired? Not at all. Behold, again the witness to truth, that reproving sword of the Spirit, the freest tongue of piety, lives, and is not dead; loosed, not bound, it cries against you more clearly than the blood of Abel: 'It is not lawful for you to have the wife of your brother Philip' (Mark 6:18). He exposes your crime, he who would hold you back from the unholy bed, who would rescue you from the crime pressing upon you in anger. Did you come to your senses? By no means. Were you chastened, did you repent? Not in the least. You did not lessen your lust: you gave your whole mind to the Maenad; as the prize of a show you brought forth on a dish the most divine head, dripping streams of blood. O monstrousness! O most shameless banquet! That same thing is in fact done even at present; even if it does not take off John's head, yet it makes the members of Christ members of a harlot. For what else do drunkenness and revelling produce, according to the Apostle's meaning?

Tell me, you too, wicked and criminal Herodias; did you gain any advantage from your reckless scheme? Did you bury the Baptist beneath the earth? Is there then no one who still contradicts and opposes you? Indeed your hope is vain, feeble the tale you played out, empty your zeal and effort. A reversal of things has come about: as much as you seemed to hide it, so much was your crime divulged. Where you thought it would lie hidden, from there your deed is handed down to generations of generations.

And you indeed perished with your husband by a bitter death, the corpses of you both rotting and stinking in the tomb and swarming with a mass of worms; but the head which you cut off leaps above the earth: the hands of saints serve it, choirs of priests escort it in procession, ranks of monks entreat it, troops of nobles magnify it and accompany it with praises. It gathers by far the greatest multitude of men, an assembly collected by the will of God; gathering together, to put it in a word, the very multitude of angels, and joining us in fellowship of praise; since, being supremely dear to the angels, the most glorious festival of him who vies with them in name and glory stands equal with theirs. It gushes forth ointments of grace above nard, above saffron, above cinnamon and all the perfumers' spices. It cries out and shouts, exposing without a voice your scheme, ever full of crime.

Such is the end of wickedness, and such great infamy accompanies it. Understand this, you too, kings of the earth, satraps and powerful men, governors and subjects, and the whole race of men, so that, following what is lawful in marriages as in other things, you may not fall into the same guilt as those criminals, disfigured by like disgrace.

But since we have crowned the golden head, as far as was granted, with flowers of praise more precious than gold, come, I pray, let us likewise take up the other members too, lest by praising the forerunner in part we seem to offer a diminished praise, less than is just. What then is more splendid and shining than the hands which were found worthy to be laid on Christ in baptism? For since God is fire, consider that by the touch of the divine crown, as by contact with fire, it came about that the forerunner's hands, their nature in no way changed, were made fiery. His back 'in the paleness of gold', as is sung (Ps. 67:14), since he carried the cross of Christ on his shoulders. His belly 'an ivory box upon a sapphire stone' (Song 5:14), as Scripture says, since he banished the delights of the belly that lie in the navel. His loins embraced the holiness of chastity, since he obtained the gift of virginity. 'The joints of his thighs like necklaces' (Song 7:2), since he was girded with the sword of imperturbability. His legs 'pillars of marble set upon bases of gold' (Song 5:15), that is, of the virtues. His feet having divine steps, since he prepared the paths of the Lord. All the members of that most sacred and most unblemished body are arms of righteousness: a chosen vessel, sanctified. Chastity reared it to manhood, constant prayer perfected it. Nor should I leave out even what is external, namely his garment and belt. Indeed the patriarch Jacob had made a many-coloured tunic for Joseph, his dearest son, but the great evangelist Matthew describes John's garment as simple and in no way elaborate. For he says, 'His clothing of camels' hair, and a leather belt around his loins' (Matt. 3:4); darkly indicating by this too the symbols that bring the death of sin: although there the many-coloured garment is also explained in another sense. But what mind and tongue could be equal for me to have my fill of your praise in each member, O greatest glory of men? But since I am constrained and needy on both counts, as most kind may you grant pardon, and strengthen me first of all, your least servant, together with my spiritual father and your flock, and keep safe all the praisers of your divine magnificence, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and dominion with the most holy Father and the life-giving Spirit, now and always, and for ages of ages. Amen.
